R.name: Prosecution of Offenses
R.hook: Who files, what goes in it, where, and when you may change it.
mem: Complaint = **sworn** written statement by the offended party, a peace officer, or a public officer enforcing the law violated.
Information = written accusation **subscribed by the prosecutor**, filed in court. It need **not** be sworn.
Institution of the case (filing for PI, or filing in court) **interrupts prescription**, unless a special law says otherwise.

items: Name of the accused
Designation of the offense by statute
Acts or omissions complained of
Name of the offended party
Approximate date
Place of the offense

doc: **Qualifying and aggravating** circumstances must be alleged in the information, or they cannot be appreciated (Secs. 8–9).
**One offense only** (duplicity), unless the law gives a single penalty for several offenses (Sec. 13).

**Venue** (Sec. 15): where the offense or any essential ingredient happened. Vehicle or aircraft: anywhere it passed, including departure and arrival. Vessel: first port of entry or any place it passed. Art. 2 RPC crimes: the court where first filed.
All cases are under the **direction and control of the public prosecutor**. A private prosecutor may act with written authority (heavy workload or no prosecutor), subject to court approval.
Offended party may **intervene by counsel** if the civil action was not waived, reserved, or filed separately (Sec. 16).

head: Crime
Who files
Notes
rows: Must include BOTH guilty parties if alive; barred if he consented or pardoned
Offended party, or her parents, grandparents, guardian (in that order)
A minor may file on her own; barred if expressly pardoned
Prosecutor may file without a complaint

items: General rule: **any amendment, in form or substance, without leave**.
Exception: an amendment that **downgrades** the offense or **drops an accused** needs a motion by the prosecutor, **notice to the offended party**, and **leave of court**.
Only **formal** amendments, **with leave**, and **without prejudice** to the accused. A substantial amendment (e.g., homicide → murder) is not allowed.
**Substitution:** if the wrong offense was charged, the court dismisses the original once the proper information is filed, provided there is no double jeopardy.

R.trap: An information is valid even if not sworn. A complaint must be sworn.

R.name: Prosecution of Civil Action
R.hook: Civil rides with criminal — unless waived, reserved, or filed first.
mem: The civil action ex delicto is **deemed instituted** with the criminal action, unless the offended party **waives** it, **reserves** it, or **files it ahead**.
Reservation must be made **before the prosecution starts presenting evidence**.
**B.P. 22:** the civil action is always included. **No reservation allowed.** Filing fees are based on the amount of the check.
doc: No counterclaim, cross-claim, or third-party complaint in the criminal case.

**Suspension (Sec. 2):** once the criminal case starts, the separate civil action ex delicto cannot proceed until final judgment in the criminal case. A civil case filed earlier is suspended; it may be consolidated.
**Acquittal** does not end civil liability, unless the judgment finds the act from which it arises **did not exist**.
**Independent civil actions** (Arts. 32, 33, 34, 2176 Civil Code) proceed on their own and need only preponderance of evidence. No double recovery. Jurisprudence: no reservation needed.
A final civil judgment for the defendant does not bar the criminal case (Sec. 5).

head: When
Effect
rows: Case dismissed; civil action may be filed against the estate
Criminal and civil ex delicto liability extinguished; independent civil action continues against the estate
Criminal liability and civil liability based solely on the crime extinguished; civil liability from other sources survives

items: The **previously instituted** civil action involves an issue similar or intimately related to the issue in the later criminal action.
Its resolution **determines whether the criminal action may proceed**.

doc2: File the petition to suspend with the prosecutor during PI, or in the criminal case **before the prosecution rests** (Sec. 6).
R.trap: A civil case filed AFTER the criminal case cannot be a prejudicial question.

R.name: Preliminary Investigation
mem: PI required when the penalty is **at least 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day**, regardless of fine.
Officer: within **10 days** dismiss or subpoena. Respondent: counter-affidavit in **10 days**. **No motion to dismiss** in place of a counter-affidavit.
Resolution: forward in **5 days**; head prosecutor acts in **10 days**.
Judge: evaluate within **10 days** of filing; may require more evidence in **5 days**; resolve in **30 days**.

req.t: Before an information is filed or dismissed
items: **Prior written authority or approval** of the provincial/city prosecutor, chief state prosecutor, or Ombudsman (Sec. 4).

doc: PI is a **statutory** right but part of due process. Its **absence does not affect jurisdiction** or the validity of the information. It is **waived** if not raised **before plea**. Remedy: ask the court to suspend and remand for PI.

**Inquest (Sec. 6):** a person lawfully arrested without a warrant may be charged without PI after inquest. Before filing, he may ask for PI by **waiving Art. 125 RPC with counsel**; PI must end in **15 days**; he may still apply for bail. After filing, he may ask for PI within **5 days** of learning of the filing.
The Secretary of Justice may reverse or modify the prosecutor's resolution.
MTC judges no longer conduct PI (A.M. No. 05-8-26-SC).

exc.t: No warrant of arrest needed when…
items: The accused is already detained under a warrant from an MTC judge.
The case was filed after inquest (Sec. 6).
The offense is punishable by fine only.

R.trap: Exactly 4 years and 2 months → no PI. It must be at least 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day.

R.name: Arrest
R.hook: No warrant only if: saw it, it just happened plus personal knowledge, or an escapee.

items: **In flagrante:** in the officer's presence, the person has committed, is committing, or is attempting an offense — an **overt act** is needed.
**Hot pursuit:** an offense **has just been committed** and the officer has probable cause based on **personal knowledge** of facts that this person did it.
**Escapee** from a penal establishment or while being transferred.

mem: Warrant executed within **10 days** of receipt; officer reports within **10 days** after that period.
Arrest may be made **any day, any time** of day or night (Sec. 6).
doc: A tip alone, with no overt act seen by the officers, is not in flagrante.
Objection to an illegal arrest is **waived** if not raised **before plea**. An illegal arrest does not affect the court's jurisdiction over the case.
Even if the arrest objection is waived, evidence from an **illegal search remains inadmissible**.
A warrant of arrest has **no expiry**; it stays valid until served or lifted.
An escaped person may be retaken without a warrant anywhere in the Philippines (Sec. 13).

exc.t: The officer need not state the cause of arrest when…
items: The person flees or forcibly resists before he can be told.
Telling him would imperil the arrest.
(Without warrant) he is caught in the act or pursued right after.

R.trap: Waiving the illegal arrest does NOT make illegally seized evidence admissible.

R.name: Bail
R.hook: Before RTC conviction: right. After: discretion. RP plus strong evidence: no bail.

head: Situation
Bail
rows: Before or after conviction by MTC
Before RTC conviction, offense NOT punishable by RP, life, or death
Charged with offense punishable by RP, life, or death
Denied if evidence of guilt is strong (hearing required)
After RTC conviction, offense not RP/life/death
No bail (except probation applied for before finality)

req.t: Deny or cancel bail pending appeal when penalty imposed exceeds 6 years AND any of these is shown (Sec. 5)
items: Recidivist, quasi-recidivist, habitual delinquent, or crime aggravated by reiteration
Previously escaped, evaded sentence, or violated bail conditions without valid reason
Committed the offense while on probation, parole, or conditional pardon
Probability of flight
Undue risk of committing another crime during appeal

doc: The **prosecution has the burden** to show evidence of guilt is strong (Sec. 8). A **hearing is mandatory**, even if the prosecutor does not object.
Bail requires **custody of the law** (actual or constructive).

**Where to file (Sec. 17):** where the case is pending; if the judge is absent, any RTC/MTC judge in the area; if arrested elsewhere, any RTC judge there (MTC if none). Discretionary bail and recognizance: **only** where the case is pending. Not yet charged: any court where held.
**Sec. 16:** detained for the maximum penalty → release; destierro → release after **30 days**; detained for the minimum → reduced bail or recognizance.
**Forfeiture:** bondsmen get **30 days** to produce the accused and explain.
**Sec. 26:** applying for bail does **not** waive objections to the arrest, the warrant, or the PI, if raised **before plea**.

items: The trial court may act on it even after a notice of appeal, **if it has not yet transmitted the records**.
If the trial court **changed the offense from non-bailable to bailable**, only the **appellate court** may act on the application.

R.trap: Bail granted without a hearing in an RP case is void, even if the prosecutor did not object.

R.name: Rights of the Accused at Trial
R.hook: Presumed innocent, informed, present, heard, confronting, speedy.
doc: Presumed innocent until proven guilty **beyond reasonable doubt**.
Present and defend in person and by counsel **from arraignment to promulgation**.
Testify for himself (cross limited to matters on direct); silence not held against him; not compelled to testify against himself.
Confront and cross-examine witnesses; compulsory process; speedy, impartial, public trial; appeal.

items: Accused has been **arraigned**
Accused was **duly notified**
His absence is **unjustified**
Arraignment and plea
Promulgation of a judgment of conviction (except light offenses)
When the court orders it for **identification**

Prior testimony of a witness who is **dead, abroad, cannot be found, or unable to testify**, given in another case with the **same parties and subject matter**, where the adverse party **had the chance to cross-examine**.

R.trap: Trial in absentia needs arraignment first. An unarraigned accused cannot be tried in absentia.

R.name: Arraignment and Plea
R.hook: In open court, in person, in a language he understands.
mem: Arraignment within **30 days** from the court acquiring jurisdiction over the accused.
Detained accused: raffle and records within **3 days**; arraignment within **10 days** from raffle; pre-trial within **10 days** after arraignment.
Suspension for a pending petition for review at the DOJ/OP: **60 days** maximum.

cls.t: What the court does with each plea
head: Plea
Result
rows: Plea deemed withdrawn; not guilty entered
Searching inquiry + prosecution MUST prove guilt and degree of culpability

doc: The accused **must be present** and plead **personally**.

**Plea to a lesser offense (Sec. 2):** with consent of the **offended party and prosecutor**, at arraignment; or after arraignment but before trial by withdrawing the not-guilty plea. No amendment needed. If the offended party fails to appear despite notice, the prosecutor's consent alone suffices (Sec. 1(f)).
**Improvident plea** of guilty may be withdrawn any time **before the judgment becomes final**.
**Bill of particulars:** move **before arraignment**, specifying the defects.
The court must inform the accused of his right to counsel and appoint counsel de oficio if needed.

items: Unsound mental condition making him unable to understand the charge
Prejudicial question exists
Petition for review pending at the DOJ or OP (max 60 days)

R.trap: A counsel cannot enter the plea for the accused; the accused pleads personally.

R.name: Motion to Quash
R.hook: Raise it before plea or lose it — except for four grounds.

head: Ground
rows: Facts charged do not constitute an offense
Officer who filed had no authority
Averments show a legal excuse or justification

mem: File **before plea**, in writing, stating the grounds. The court considers only stated grounds, **except lack of jurisdiction over the offense**.
**Never waived:** (a) no offense, (b) no jurisdiction over offense, (g) extinction, (i) double jeopardy.
Quash granted → new information may be filed, **except** on grounds (g) extinction and (i) double jeopardy.
Provisional dismissal becomes permanent: **1 year** (penalty ≤ 6 years or fine only); **2 years** (penalty > 6 years).

req.t: Double jeopardy — first jeopardy attached when
items: Valid complaint or information
Court of competent jurisdiction
Accused **arraigned and pleaded**
Accused **convicted, acquitted, or case dismissed/terminated without his express consent**

doc: The second prosecution is barred if it is for the **same offense**, its attempt or frustration, or an offense that **necessarily includes or is included** in it.
Defect curable by amendment → court orders amendment before quashing (Sec. 4).
**Provisional dismissal** needs the accused's **express consent** and **notice to the offended party** (Sec. 8).
Jurisprudence (Gomez v. People, 2020): lack of the head prosecutor's prior written approval is **waivable**.

exc.t: Dismissal does NOT bar refiling when…
items: The case was dismissed **with the accused's express consent** (e.g., on his motion).
**Insufficiency of evidence** (e.g., demurrer granted), or
**Denial of the right to speedy trial**. These act as acquittals even if the accused asked for them.

cls2.t: Conviction does not bar a graver charge when (Sec. 7)
rows: Graver offense developed from supervening facts
Facts of the graver charge were discovered only after plea
Plea to a lesser offense made without consent of prosecutor and offended party

R.trap: Credit for time served applies when he is later convicted of the graver offense.

R.name: Pre-Trial
R.hook: Mandatory, written, signed by accused AND counsel.
mem: Pre-trial is **mandatory** in criminal cases.
Within **30 days** from the court acquiring jurisdiction over the accused (detained: **10 days** after arraignment).

req.t: For a pre-trial admission to be used against the accused (Sec. 2)
items: Reduced **in writing**
Signed by the **accused**
Signed by **counsel**

doc: Matters: plea bargaining, stipulation of facts, marking of evidence, waiver of objections, modified order of trial, other matters.
Non-appearance of counsel or prosecutor without excuse → sanctions (Sec. 3).
The **pre-trial order** binds the parties and limits the trial to matters not disposed of, unless modified to prevent manifest injustice.
R.trap: An admission signed only by counsel cannot be used against the accused.

R.name: Trial
mem: At least **15 days** to prepare for trial after a not-guilty plea; trial starts within **30 days** from receipt of the pre-trial order.
Trial must not exceed **180 days** from the first day.
Demurrer: leave within **5 days** after prosecution rests (opposition **5 days**); demurrer within **10 days** from notice of leave (opposition **10 days**). All non-extendible.
New trial after order: start within **30 days**. Reopening: finish within **30 days**.

req.t: Discharge as state witness (Sec. 17) — all five
items: **Absolute necessity** for his testimony
**No other direct evidence** available
Testimony can be **substantially corroborated** in material points
He does **not appear to be the most guilty**
Never convicted of an offense involving **moral turpitude**

head: Filed
If denied
If granted
rows: Accused waives right to present evidence; case decided on prosecution evidence

doc: Denial of leave or demurrer: **not reviewable by appeal or certiorari before judgment**.
Motion to discharge must be filed **before the prosecution rests**. If denied, the sworn statement is inadmissible.
**Speedy trial dismissal (Sec. 9):** move before trial, or it is waived. Accused proves it; prosecution must show excluded delays.
**Reverse trial:** when the accused admits the act but claims a lawful defense.

**Conditional examination:** prosecution witness too sick or leaving the country → examined before the court where the case is pending. Defense witness (sick, over 100 km and no means, etc.) → before a judge, a member of the bar, or an inferior court judge.
**Sec. 19:** wrong offense charged and he cannot be convicted of it or an included offense → commit him for the proper offense and dismiss the original once the new information is filed.

items: …**unless** he fails or refuses to testify according to his sworn statement.

R.trap: Demurrer without leave + denial = no more defense evidence.

R.name: Judgment
R.hook: Charged vs proved: convict of whichever is included in the other.
doc: **Variance (Secs. 4–5):** convict of the offense **proved** if it is included in the offense charged, or of the offense **charged** if it is included in the offense proved.

Conviction must state: legal qualification and circumstances, participation, penalty, civil liability. **Acquittal** must state whether evidence **absolutely failed** or only failed to prove guilt **beyond reasonable doubt**, and whether the act giving rise to civil liability **existed**.
Two offenses in one information **without objection before trial** → convict of each proven (Sec. 3).

**Promulgation (Sec. 6):** read in the presence of the accused. Absent without justification → record in docket and serve; he **loses his remedies** and a warrant issues. Within **15 days** he may surrender and move for leave, proving justifiable cause.

items: The period to appeal lapses
Sentence is partially or totally served
Accused expressly waives appeal in writing
Accused applies for probation

R.trap: An unalleged qualifying circumstance cannot raise the crime, even if proven.

R.name: New Trial or Reconsideration
mem: Any time **before the judgment of conviction becomes final**, on the accused's motion, or by the court with his consent.

items: Discovered after trial
Not discoverable earlier with reasonable diligence
Material, not merely cumulative, corroborative, or impeaching
Likely to change the judgment

head: Ground
Effect if granted
rows: Errors of law or irregularities during trial (new trial)
Affected proceedings and evidence set aside and taken anew
Evidence already presented stands; new evidence added
Errors of law or fact in the judgment (reconsideration)
No further proceedings needed; judgment corrected

doc: In all cases the original judgment is set aside and a new one rendered.
Newly discovered evidence motions need affidavits or authenticated documents.
R.trap: The prosecution cannot move for new trial after a conviction.

R.name: Appeal
R.hook: 15 days, fresh period, and appeal reopens everything.
mem: Appeal within **15 days** from promulgation or notice of the final order.
**Fresh period rule** (Neypes, applied in Yu v. Samson-Tatad): new **15 days** from receipt of the order denying MR or MNT.
doc: Any party may appeal, unless it would place the accused in **double jeopardy**.
An appeal **opens the whole case**; the appellate court may increase the penalty.

**Sec. 11:** an appeal by one accused helps the others only if the judgment is **favorable and applicable** to them. The offended party's appeal of the civil aspect does not affect the criminal aspect. Appeal stays execution as to the appellant.
**Withdrawal (Sec. 12):** allowed before the records are forwarded; the judgment becomes final.
An **acquittal** cannot be appealed by the prosecution. Only Rule 65 for grave abuse amounting to lack of jurisdiction.
R.trap: An accused who appeals may end up with a higher penalty.

R.name: Procedure in the MTC
R.hook: Same as RTC, except where a rule applies only to the RTC or summary procedure applies.
doc: Uniform procedure: MTC cases follow the same procedure as RTC cases, except provisions that apply only to the RTC and cases under the Rule on Summary Procedure.
R.trap: Remember MTC judges no longer conduct preliminary investigations.

R.name: Procedure in the Court of Appeals
R.hook: Briefs on time — unless counsel de oficio.
mem: Appellant's brief: **30 days** from notice. Appellee's brief: **30 days** from receipt. Reply: **20 days**.
Motion for reconsideration: **15 days** from notice of the decision.
doc: **Dismissal (Sec. 8):** for failure to file the brief — **except** when the appellant has counsel de oficio. Also if the appellant **escapes, jumps bail, or flees abroad** during the appeal.
**Scope (Sec. 11):** reverse, affirm, modify, increase or reduce the penalty, remand for new trial, or dismiss.
CA imposing **RP or life**: renders and enters judgment; appeal to the SC by **notice of appeal**.
**New trial at the CA (Sec. 14):** after appeal is perfected and before the CA judgment becomes final, on newly discovered evidence.
The CA may receive evidence in limited cases (Sec. 12).

exc.t: No dismissal for failure to file a brief when…
items: The appellant is represented by **counsel de oficio**.

R.trap: Jumping bail during appeal lets the CA dismiss the appeal.

R.name: Procedure in the Supreme Court
R.hook: Tie on acquittal → deliberate again → still tied → acquit.
doc: Procedure is the same as in the CA unless the Constitution or law provides otherwise.
Review of CA decisions: petition for review on certiorari, as in civil cases.
If the SC en banc is equally divided (or no majority) on whether to acquit, the case is deliberated again; if still no decision, the **conviction is reversed and the accused acquitted** (Sec. 3).
R.trap: A tie does not affirm a conviction; it ends in acquittal.

R.name: Search and Seizure
R.hook: One offense, judge examines personally, 10 days, two local witnesses.

items: Probable cause in connection with **one specific offense**
Determined **personally by the judge**
After examining under oath the complainant and witnesses — **searching questions and answers, in writing** (Sec. 5)
**Particularly describing** the place and the things to be seized

mem: Valid for **10 days** from its date (Sec. 10).
Served in the **daytime**, unless the affidavit says the property is on the person or in the place — then any time (Sec. 9).
Search in the presence of the **occupant or family member**; if absent, **two witnesses of sufficient age and discretion residing in the same locality** (Sec. 8).
Judge checks for a return **10 days** after issuance (Sec. 12).

head: Situation
Court
rows: Any court within whose territory the crime was committed
Any court in the judicial region of the crime or where the warrant will be enforced
Only the court where the case is pending

doc: Seizable: subject of the offense; stolen or embezzled property and fruits; means used or intended to commit it (Sec. 3).
**Motion to quash warrant / suppress evidence (Sec. 14):** in the court where the case is filed; if none yet, the issuing court.
Officer may break doors or windows if refused entry after giving notice (Sec. 7). Leave a detailed receipt (Sec. 11).

items: Incident to a **lawful** arrest
**Plain view**
Moving vehicle
Consented search
Customs search
Stop and frisk
Exigent and emergency circumstances
Routine checkpoints (visual)

exx.t: Plain view needs all of these
items: Officer has a **prior valid intrusion** (lawfully present)
Evidence discovered **inadvertently**
Its illegal character is **immediately apparent**
Noticed **without further search**

R.trap: A warrant for two different offenses is a void scatter-shot warrant.

R.name: Provisional Remedies
R.hook: Only if the civil action rides with the criminal case.

items: Accused is **about to abscond** from the Philippines

Claim for money or property **embezzled or converted** by a public officer, corporate officer, attorney, factor, broker, agent, clerk, or fiduciary in the course of the job, or for willful violation of duty
Accused **concealed, removed, or disposed** of property, or is about to
Accused **resides outside** the Philippines

doc: Civil provisional remedies apply **only to the civil action deemed instituted** with the criminal case (Sec. 1).
R.trap: If the civil action was reserved or filed separately, seek attachment there, not in the criminal case.

S.title: Private crimes and who files
S.base: Maria, 17, says her uncle committed acts of lasciviousness against her. Her parents are alive. No complaint has been filed.

o: Only Maria's parents, because she is a minor
Maria herself, even without her parents
The prosecutor, by filing an information on his own
Only a court-appointed guardian
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 5: the offended party, even a minor, may file independently of her parents, grandparents, or guardian, unless she is incompetent or incapable. Acts of lasciviousness is a private crime, so the prosecutor cannot start it alone.

qs.tw: Maria refuses to file anything.
o: No, only the offended party may file
Yes. If the minor fails to file, her parents, grandparents, or guardian may file, in that order
Yes, but only with the prosecutor's written consent
No. Once the minor refuses, the case can never be filed
qs.ex: When the minor fails to file, the right passes to her parents, grandparents, or guardian. The right is exclusive and successive in that order.

qs.tw: Change the crime: the uncle raped Maria.
qs.q: Is a complaint by Maria or her family still needed to start the case?
o: Yes, rape is a private crime
No. Rape is now a crime against persons; the prosecutor may file an information
Yes, unless Maria is below 12
Only if the uncle is a public officer
qs.ex: Since R.A. 8353 (1997), rape is a crime against persons and is prosecuted like any public crime.

qs.tw: New facts: Jun catches his wife and her lover in adultery. He files a complaint against his wife only, because the lover is his business partner.
o: Yes, the offended spouse chooses whom to charge
No. He must include both guilty parties if both are alive
Yes, the prosecutor can add the lover later
No, adultery must be filed by the prosecutor
qs.ex: Adultery and concubinage: only the offended spouse may file, and he must include both guilty parties if both are alive (Rule 110, Sec. 5).

qs.tw: Same adultery facts, but before filing, Jun wrote his wife a letter forgiving her and her lover.
o: Yes, pardon only affects civil liability
No. The offended spouse cannot file if he pardoned the offenders
Yes, if within the prescriptive period
Only if the lover did not know of the pardon
qs.ex: The offended spouse cannot institute the case if he consented to or pardoned the offenders.

S.title: Amendment and variance
S.base: An information for homicide is filed against Rey. He has not been arraigned.

qs.q: The prosecutor wants to amend it to murder by alleging treachery. Does he need leave of court?
o: Yes, any substantial amendment needs leave
No. Before plea, amendments in form or substance need no leave
Yes, and the offended party must consent
No amendment is allowed; he must refile
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 14: before plea, amendments in form or substance need no leave — except amendments that downgrade the offense or drop an accused.

qs.tw: Instead, still before plea, the prosecutor wants to downgrade it to reckless imprudence resulting in homicide.
o: Nothing; amendments before plea are free
Only the accused's consent
A motion by the prosecutor, notice to the offended party, and leave of court
Approval of the Secretary of Justice
qs.ex: Downgrading the offense or excluding an accused before plea needs a motion by the prosecutor, notice to the offended party, and leave of court.

qs.tw: Rey has been arraigned for homicide and trial has started. Now the prosecutor wants to add treachery.
o: Yes, with leave of court
Yes, before the defense presents evidence
No. After plea, only formal amendments are allowed, and this one is substantial
Yes, qualifying circumstances are only formal
qs.ex: After plea, only formal amendments with leave and without prejudice. Changing homicide to murder changes the offense and penalty, so it is substantial.

qs.tw: No amendment was made. At trial, treachery is clearly proven.
qs.q: What crime may Rey be convicted of?
o: Murder, because treachery was proven
Homicide only, because treachery was not alleged
Acquittal because of the variance
Murder with a reduced penalty
qs.ex: Qualifying circumstances must be alleged (Rule 110, Secs. 8–9). Under Rule 120, Sec. 4, he is convicted of the offense charged (homicide), which is included in the offense proved (murder).

qs.tw: Reverse it: the information charges murder with treachery, but treachery is not proven.
o: Acquittal, because murder was not proven
Conviction for homicide, which is included in murder
Dismissal and refiling as homicide
Conviction for murder, because the information says so
qs.ex: When the offense charged (murder) necessarily includes the offense proved (homicide), he is convicted of the offense proved.

S.title: The civil action riding along
S.base: A bus hits Ana. She files a criminal complaint for reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries against the driver. She says nothing about a civil case.

qs.q: Is her civil claim based on the crime included in the criminal case?
o: No, she must file a separate civil case
Yes. It is deemed instituted unless she waives, reserves, or files it ahead
Only if she pays docket fees first
Only if the prosecutor asks for damages
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1: the civil action ex delicto is deemed instituted with the criminal action unless waived, reserved, or filed earlier.

qs.tw: Before the prosecution presents evidence, Ana reserves and files a separate civil action ex delicto against the driver.
qs.q: Can the civil case proceed while the criminal case is pending?
o: Yes, side by side
No. It is suspended until final judgment in the criminal case
Yes, but only up to pre-trial
No, it must be dismissed
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 2: the separate civil action arising from the offense cannot proceed until final judgment in the criminal case.

qs.tw: Instead, Ana sues the driver for quasi-delict under Art. 2176. She made no reservation.
qs.q: Can this civil case proceed while the criminal case is pending?
o: No, it is suspended
No, because she did not reserve it
Yes. It is an independent civil action
Yes, but only after arraignment
qs.ex: Independent civil actions (Arts. 32, 33, 34, 2176) proceed on their own, on preponderance of evidence (Rule 111, Sec. 3). No reservation needed. No double recovery.

qs.tw: Back to the criminal case with the civil action included. The driver is acquitted on reasonable doubt.
qs.q: Can the court still order him to pay damages?
o: No, acquittal always ends civil liability
Yes, if civil liability is proven by preponderance of evidence
Only if Ana files a new civil case
No, unless he admits fault
qs.ex: Acquittal ends civil liability only if the judgment finds the act from which it arises did not exist (Rule 111, Sec. 2; Rule 120, Sec. 2).

qs.tw: Change it: the court acquits because someone else was driving, not the accused.
qs.q: Is his civil liability ex delicto extinguished?
o: No, civil liability always survives
Yes. The court found he did not commit the act that gives rise to civil liability
Only if Ana appeals
No, reckless imprudence is a quasi-offense
qs.ex: When the acquittal rests on a finding that the accused did not commit the act, his civil liability arising from the crime is extinguished. Compare with reasonable doubt.

qs.tw: The driver dies after arraignment, while trial is ongoing.
o: The case continues against his estate for both liabilities
Criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto are extinguished; an independent civil action may continue against his estate
Everything is suspended until heirs are substituted
Only the criminal case ends; civil ex delicto continues in the same case
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 4: death after arraignment extinguishes the civil liability arising from the delict; independent civil actions continue against the estate.

S.title: Preliminary investigation and inquest
S.base: Police catch Dodong in the act of selling shabu and arrest him without a warrant. The offense carries more than 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day.

qs.q: Can an information be filed without a preliminary investigation?
o: No, PI is always required at this penalty
Yes, after an inquest is conducted
Yes, but only if Dodong consents
No, police must first get a warrant
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 6: a person lawfully arrested without a warrant may be charged without PI, provided an inquest was conducted.

qs.tw: Before the information is filed, Dodong asks for a regular PI.
o: Nothing; PI is his right
Sign a waiver of Art. 125 of the RPC in the presence of counsel
Post bail first
File a motion with the RTC
qs.ex: He must waive Art. 125 RPC with counsel. He may still apply for bail, and the PI must end within 15 days.

qs.tw: The information was already filed after inquest. Dodong learns of it and wants a PI.
qs.q: Within what period must he ask?
o: 15 days from arraignment
5 days from learning of the filing
Any time before trial
10 days from arrest
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 6: within 5 days from learning of the filing. A later motion is prohibited under the Continuous Trial Guidelines.

qs.tw: Dodong never asked for PI. He was arraigned and pleaded not guilty. During trial, he claims the case is void for lack of PI.
o: Yes, lack of PI is jurisdictional
No. The right is waived if not raised before plea, and its absence does not affect jurisdiction
Yes, the information must be quashed
No, drug cases never need PI
qs.ex: Absence of PI does not affect the court's jurisdiction or the information's validity. The right is waived if not invoked before plea.

qs.tw: New case: a complaint for an offense with a maximum penalty of exactly 4 years and 2 months.
o: Yes, 4 years and up needs PI
No. PI is required only when the penalty is at least 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day
Yes, because the accused is not detained
Only if the complainant asks
qs.ex: The threshold is at least 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day, regardless of fine. One day short means no PI.

S.title: Arrest and search
S.base: Police get a tip that Xander carries shabu in a red bag at a bus terminal. Without a warrant, they stop him, open his bag, find shabu, and then arrest him.

o: Yes, because shabu was found
No. A tip alone, with no overt act in the officers' presence, does not justify an in flagrante arrest
Yes, under hot pursuit
Yes, because he was in a public place
qs.ex: In flagrante needs an overt act showing a crime in the officer's presence. Here the search came first and created the basis for arrest. The shabu is inadmissible.

qs.tw: Xander's lawyer does not object to the arrest before arraignment.
o: The shabu becomes admissible
Objections to the arrest are waived, but the shabu from the illegal search stays inadmissible
The case must be dismissed
Nothing; arrest objections can be raised anytime
qs.ex: Failure to object before plea waives the illegality of the arrest. It does not cure the inadmissibility of illegally seized evidence.

qs.tw: Change the facts: officers personally see Xander hand a sachet to a buyer and receive money.
qs.q: Are the arrest and search of his person valid?
o: No, they still needed a warrant
Yes. In flagrante arrest, and search incident to a lawful arrest
Only the arrest is valid
Only if a barangay official was present
qs.ex: The overt act happened in their presence (Rule 113, Sec. 5(a)). A lawfully arrested person may be searched without a warrant (Rule 126, Sec. 13).

qs.tw: New facts: police hold a search warrant for Xander's house dated 12 days ago. They search today.
o: Yes, warrants do not expire
No. A search warrant is valid only 10 days from its date
Yes, if done in daytime
Yes, if the judge extends it orally
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 10: valid for 10 days, then void. Contrast: a warrant of arrest does not expire.

qs.tw: The warrant is valid. Xander's family is away, so police search with two members of the raiding team as witnesses.
o: Yes, any two adults may witness
No. Without the occupant or family, the witnesses must be two persons of sufficient age and discretion residing in the same locality
Yes, police are public officers
No, a search can never proceed without the owner
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 8. Raiding officers do not qualify as the two local witnesses.

qs.tw: Suppose the warrant authorized a search for violations of both the drugs law and the firearms law.
o: Nothing
It covers more than one specific offense, so it is a void scatter-shot warrant
It should name the judge's branch
It needed the prosecutor's signature
qs.ex: Rule 126, Sec. 4: a search warrant may issue only in connection with one specific offense.

S.title: Bail at every stage
S.base: Ella is charged in the RTC with murder (punishable by reclusion perpetua). She is detained.

qs.q: Is bail a matter of right?
o: Yes, before conviction bail is always a right
No. It may be denied if evidence of guilt is strong, and a hearing is required
Yes, if she can pay
No, murder is never bailable
qs.ex: Offenses punishable by RP, life, or death are not bailable when evidence of guilt is strong (Sec. 7). The prosecution has the burden (Sec. 8).

qs.tw: The prosecutor does not object and presents no evidence. The judge grants bail without a hearing.
o: Yes, the prosecution waived
No. A hearing is mandatory, even without objection
Yes, if the bail amount is high
No, only the CA may grant bail here
qs.ex: For RP offenses, the judge must hold a hearing to determine whether evidence of guilt is strong, with notice to the prosecutor.

qs.tw: After trial, the RTC convicts Ella only of homicide and sentences her to 12 years. She appeals and applies for bail.
qs.q: Which court resolves her bail application?
o: The RTC, if it still has the records
Only the appellate court, because the judgment changed the offense from non-bailable to bailable
No court; bail is denied after conviction
The RTC, with the prosecutor's consent
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 5: if the trial court changed the nature of the offense from non-bailable to bailable, only the appellate court may act on bail.

qs.tw: Another accused, Fe, was charged with homicide from the start. The RTC convicts her with 8 years. The prosecution shows she is a recidivist.
qs.q: What happens to her bail pending appeal?
o: Granted as a matter of right
Denied, because the penalty exceeds 6 years and she is a recidivist
Granted, because homicide is bailable
Referred to the Supreme Court
qs.ex: After RTC conviction, bail is discretionary. Penalty over 6 years plus a Sec. 5 circumstance (recidivism) → bail denied or cancelled.

qs.tw: Rewind: before any conviction, Fe (charged with homicide) is arrested in Cebu on a warrant from a Manila RTC.
o: Only in the Manila RTC
In the Manila RTC, or with any RTC judge in Cebu (or MTC judge if no RTC judge is available)
Only with the Supreme Court
At the police station
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 17(a): bail as a matter of right may be filed where the case is pending, or with an RTC judge where arrested (MTC if none available).

qs.tw: Fe's conviction has become final. She did not apply for probation.
o: Yes, bail is always available
No. There is no bail after the judgment of conviction becomes final
Yes, if the amount is doubled
Yes, if she files a petition for review
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 24. Exception: an application for probation filed before finality lets her stay on bail.

S.title: Arraignment and motion to quash
S.base: An assistant prosecutor filed an information against Gary without the prior written approval of the city prosecutor.

qs.q: What is Gary's remedy before arraignment?
o: Motion for bill of particulars
Motion to quash: the officer who filed had no authority
Petition for certiorari in the CA
Motion for reconsideration
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(d), with Rule 112, Sec. 4: no information may be filed without the head prosecutor's prior written approval.

qs.tw: Gary is arraigned and pleads not guilty. Only then does he move to quash on that ground.
o: Yes, lack of authority can be raised anytime
No. This ground is waived if not raised before plea
Yes, it is jurisdictional
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Only four grounds survive a plea (Rule 117, Sec. 9). Gomez v. People (2020) treats lack of prior approval as waivable.

qs.tw: Instead, after plea, Gary moves to quash because the facts alleged do not constitute an offense.
o: Yes, all grounds are waived after plea
No. It is one of the grounds never waived
Yes, unless the court allows it
No, but he must first withdraw his plea
qs.ex: Never waived: (a) no offense, (b) no jurisdiction over the offense, (g) extinction, (i) double jeopardy.

qs.tw: At arraignment, Gary says: "Guilty, but I only did it to defend myself."
o: Valid guilty plea with a mitigating circumstance
The plea is deemed withdrawn and a plea of not guilty is entered
The court keeps asking until he picks one
A conditional plea the court may accept
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 1(d): a guilty plea with exculpatory evidence is deemed withdrawn; not guilty is entered.

qs.tw: The charge is murder and Gary voluntarily pleads guilty.
o: Convict him immediately
Conduct a searching inquiry and require the prosecution to prove guilt and the precise degree of culpability
Ask the offended party for consent
Reject the plea
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 3: capital offense → searching inquiry plus mandatory prosecution evidence. Non-capital → evidence is discretionary (Sec. 4).

qs.tw: Gary's motion to quash is granted because the information charged two offenses.
qs.q: Can the prosecutor file a new information?
o: No, the quash bars any new case
Yes. A quash does not bar refiling unless based on extinction of liability or double jeopardy
Only with leave of the CA
Only if the accused consents
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 6.

S.title: Double jeopardy and dismissals
S.base: Hector is charged with serious physical injuries (penalty not over 6 years). He is arraigned and pleads not guilty.

qs.q: Prosecution witnesses keep failing to appear. On Hector's motion, the court dismisses for violation of his right to speedy trial. Can the case be refiled?
o: Yes, because Hector himself moved to dismiss
No. A dismissal for denial of speedy trial is an acquittal, even on the accused's motion
Yes, within one year
Only with new evidence
qs.ex: Dismissal with the accused's consent normally allows refiling — except when based on insufficiency of evidence or denial of speedy trial.

qs.tw: Instead, Hector and the prosecutor jointly ask for a provisional dismissal because they are settling. The offended party is notified, and the court grants it.
qs.q: What is the status of the case?
o: Acquittal
Provisional dismissal with his express consent; it can be revived within the time bar
Void because the offended party did not consent
Permanently dismissed right away
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 8: express consent of the accused plus notice to the offended party. Jeopardy does not attach because he consented.

qs.tw: The prosecutor revives the case 14 months after the provisional dismissal order.
o: Yes, within 2 years
No. For penalties not over 6 years, the dismissal became permanent after 1 year
Yes, there is no time limit
Only with leave of court
qs.ex: Permanent after 1 year (penalty ≤ 6 years or fine) or 2 years (penalty > 6 years).

qs.tw: Different path: Hector is convicted and serves part of his sentence. The victim later dies from those injuries.
qs.q: Can Hector now be charged with homicide?
o: No, double jeopardy bars it
Yes. A graver offense developed from a supervening fact; he is credited for time served
Yes, if he consents
No, the death is irrelevant
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(a).

qs.tw: Different path: Hector is acquitted. The prosecution appeals, arguing the judge misread the evidence.
o: Yes, the State may appeal
No. An acquittal is final; only Rule 65 for grave abuse amounting to lack of jurisdiction, not errors in weighing evidence
Yes, within 15 days
Yes, if the offended party joins
qs.ex: Finality-of-acquittal rule. Only a void acquittal (e.g., prosecution denied due process, sham trial) may be set aside.

S.title: Trial: state witness and demurrer
S.base: Ivan, Jojo, and Ken are charged with robbery. The prosecution is presenting its evidence.

qs.q: Before resting, the prosecution moves to discharge Jojo as a state witness. Jojo was previously convicted of estafa. Can Jojo be discharged?
o: He may be discharged if his testimony is absolutely necessary
He cannot be discharged; he was convicted of an offense involving moral turpitude
He may be discharged if he consents
He may be discharged if Ivan and Ken agree
qs.ex: All five requisites of Rule 119, Sec. 17 must be met, including no prior conviction for an offense involving moral turpitude. Estafa is one.

qs.tw: Ken is discharged instead. On the stand, he refuses to testify according to his sworn statement.
o: No, his discharge was an acquittal
Yes. Discharge is not an acquittal if he refuses to testify according to his sworn statement
Only for perjury
No, jeopardy attached
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 18.

qs.tw: The prosecution rests. Ivan files a demurrer without leave of court. It is denied.
o: Ivan presents his evidence
Ivan loses the right to present evidence; the case is decided on the prosecution's evidence
Ivan may appeal the denial
The case is dismissed
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 23: without leave + denied = waiver of the right to present evidence.

qs.tw: Instead, Ivan first asked for leave within 5 days, got it, filed the demurrer, and it was denied.
o: He cannot present evidence
He may present his evidence
He may file certiorari against the denial right away
He must plead guilty
qs.ex: With leave + denied = he may present evidence. The denial cannot be reviewed by appeal or certiorari before judgment.

qs.tw: The demurrer is granted. The prosecution files a Rule 65 petition, saying the judge weighed the evidence wrongly.
o: Yes, certiorari corrects any error
No. A granted demurrer is an acquittal; weighing evidence wrongly is an error of judgment, not grave abuse
Yes, if filed within 60 days
Only if the offended party files it
qs.ex: A granted demurrer is an acquittal on the merits. Certiorari lies only for grave abuse amounting to lack of jurisdiction.

S.title: Judgment, new trial, and appeal
S.base: Lito is convicted of estafa by the RTC. Notice of promulgation was properly served on him.

qs.q: Lito does not attend promulgation and has no justifiable reason. What happens?
o: Promulgation is reset until he appears
The judgment is recorded and served; he loses his remedies and a warrant issues, unless within 15 days he surrenders and shows justifiable cause
The judgment is void
He is acquitted
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: promulgation in absentia.

qs.tw: Lito attends. On day 10 he files a motion for reconsideration. He receives the denial today.
qs.q: How long does he have to appeal?
o: 5 days — the balance of 15
A fresh 15 days from receipt of the denial
30 days
None; the MR used the period
qs.ex: Fresh period rule (Neypes) applies in criminal cases (Yu v. Samson-Tatad).

qs.tw: Instead, the prosecution moves for a new trial to present evidence that would increase the penalty.
o: Yes, either party may ask
No. New trial is on the accused's motion, or by the court only with his consent
Yes, before finality
Only if the offended party joins
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 1. Reopening a conviction to raise the penalty would violate double jeopardy.

qs.tw: Lito appeals; his co-accused Mon does not. The CA acquits Lito, finding there was no deceit, so no estafa at all.
o: No, Mon did not appeal
Yes, because it is favorable and applicable to him
Only if Mon files his own appeal
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(a).

qs.tw: Instead, the CA affirms the conviction but increases the penalty.
o: No, double jeopardy
Yes. An appeal opens the whole case, and the CA may increase or reduce the penalty
Only if the prosecution also appealed
Only the SC may increase penalties
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 11. By appealing, the accused waives double jeopardy protection.

qs.tw: While the appeal is pending, Lito jumps bail.
o: Nothing; the appeal continues
Dismiss the appeal, on motion or on its own
Increase the penalty automatically
Order a new trial
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 8.

qs.tw: Rewind: right after promulgation, Lito applied for probation. Within 15 days he changes his mind and files a notice of appeal.
o: Yes, still within 15 days
No. The judgment became final when he applied for probation
Yes, if probation is denied
Only with leave of court
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 7: a judgment becomes final when the accused applies for probation.

S.title: Provisional remedies
S.base: Nora, a company cashier, is charged with estafa for converting company funds she received in her job.

qs.q: Can the company ask for preliminary attachment of Nora's property in the criminal case?
o: No, attachment is only for civil cases
Yes, if the civil action is deemed instituted, because the claim is for money converted by an employee in the course of her job
Only if she is about to leave the country
Only after conviction
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 2(b).

qs.tw: The company had earlier reserved its right to file a separate civil action.
qs.q: Can it still get attachment in the criminal case?
o: Yes, attachment is always available
No. Provisional remedies in the criminal case are only for the civil action deemed instituted with it
Yes, with a bigger bond
Only on the prosecutor's motion
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 1. It should seek attachment in its separate civil case.

qs.tw: Different case: an accused in a physical injuries case, with the civil action included, starts selling all his land to avoid paying damages.
o: No, only embezzlement cases qualify
Yes. The accused is disposing of his property, or about to
Only after conviction
Only if he is a public officer
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 2(c).

qs.tw: Instead, the accused lives abroad.
o: No, the court has no power over foreign residents
Yes. The accused resides outside the Philippines
Only if he owns no property here
Only with DFA approval
qs.ex: Rule 127, Sec. 2(d). Another ground: the accused is about to abscond from the Philippines (Sec. 2(a)).

S.title: What the information must say, and where to file
S.base: An information charges Paolo with estafa. It names the offended party, describes the acts, and says the crime happened "on or about March 2026" in Quezon City.

qs.q: The information gives only an approximate date. Is it defective?
o: Yes, the exact date is always required
No. An approximate date is enough unless the date is a material ingredient of the offense
Yes, unless the accused consents
No, the date is never needed
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 11: it is enough to state the approximate date, unless the precise date is a material ingredient of the offense.

qs.tw: The caption calls the crime "theft," but the facts described in the body are those of estafa.
qs.q: What crime is Paolo actually charged with?
o: Theft, because the caption controls
Estafa, because the facts alleged in the body control, not the caption or designation
Neither; the information is void
Both theft and estafa
qs.ex: Jurisprudence: the nature of the crime is determined by the facts alleged in the information, not by its caption or the designation of the offense.

qs.tw: The deceit happened in Makati, and Paolo received the money in Quezon City. The information is filed in Manila, where the victim lives.
o: Yes, the victim's residence is a proper venue
No. Venue is where the offense or any of its essential ingredients happened — Makati or Quezon City
Yes, if the accused does not object
Yes, any RTC in Metro Manila may hear it
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 15(a). In criminal cases venue is jurisdictional, so the Manila court has no jurisdiction over the offense.

qs.tw: New information: it charges Paolo with estafa and, separately, slight physical injuries in a different incident. He does not object before trial, and both are proven.
o: Convict only for the first offense
Convict him of both and impose a penalty for each, stating findings separately
Dismiss the whole case for duplicity
Order the prosecutor to file a new information first
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 3: if the accused fails to object to duplicity before trial, he may be convicted of as many offenses as are charged and proved.

qs.tw: Same two-offense information, but this time Paolo moves to quash before plea.
o: Denied; duplicity is only formal
Granted on the ground that more than one offense is charged; the prosecutor may file proper informations
Granted, and no new case may be filed
Denied unless the offended party agrees
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(f) and Sec. 6: a quash for duplicity does not bar refiling. Rule 110, Sec. 13 requires one offense per information unless the law gives a single penalty.

qs.tw: New case: Paolo is charged with murder. The information says "with treachery" but states no facts showing treachery. He never moved to quash or asked for a bill of particulars.
qs.q: If treachery is proven at trial, can it be appreciated?
o: No, the bare word "treachery" is never enough
Yes. By not moving to quash or asking for a bill of particulars, he waived the defect
No, the information is void
Only if he pleads guilty
qs.ex: People v. Solar (2019): an information should state the facts that make up a qualifying circumstance. An accused who does not object through a motion to quash or a bill of particulars waives the defect.

S.title: The public prosecutor and the private lawyer
S.base: Quinn is the offended party in an estafa case. She hires a private lawyer. The public prosecutor is handling the case.

qs.q: Can Quinn's private lawyer appear in the case?
o: No, only the public prosecutor may appear
Yes. The offended party may intervene by counsel, since the civil action was not waived, reserved, or filed separately
Only after conviction
Only with the accused's consent
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 16.

qs.tw: Quinn had earlier reserved her right to file a separate civil action.
qs.q: Can her private lawyer still intervene in the criminal case?
o: Yes, intervention is always allowed
No. Intervention is allowed only when the civil action was not waived, reserved, or filed separately
Yes, but only to cross-examine
Only if the public prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 16.

qs.tw: Back to no reservation. The public prosecutor is absent at a hearing. The private lawyer presents prosecution witnesses on the criminal aspect without any written authority.
o: Yes, the private lawyer represents the offended party
No. The case is under the public prosecutor's direction and control; a private prosecutor needs written authority from the head prosecutor, subject to court approval
Yes, if the judge allows it orally
Yes, for light offenses only
qs.ex: Rule 110, Sec. 5 (as amended): the private prosecutor may prosecute only with written authority of the Chief of the Prosecution Office or the Regional State Prosecutor, approved by the court.

qs.tw: After a DOJ review finds no probable cause, the public prosecutor moves to withdraw the information. The court already has the case.
qs.q: Must the judge grant the motion?
o: Yes, the prosecutor controls the case
No. Once filed in court, the case's fate rests with the court, which must make its own assessment
Yes, if the Secretary of Justice ordered it
No, withdrawals are never allowed
qs.ex: Crespo v. Mogul: once the information is filed, any disposition of the case rests in the sound discretion of the court.

qs.tw: The court dismisses the criminal case. The public prosecutor does nothing. Quinn wants to appeal the criminal aspect herself.
o: Yes, the offended party may appeal both aspects
No. Only the OSG represents the People on the criminal aspect; she may appeal only the civil aspect
Yes, if she pays docket fees
Only with the judge's permission
qs.ex: The criminal aspect belongs to the State, represented on appeal by the Solicitor General. Rule 122, Sec. 11(b): the offended party's appeal of the civil aspect does not affect the criminal aspect.

S.title: B.P. 22 and prejudicial questions
S.base: Rafa gave Sol a P500,000 check that bounced. Sol files a B.P. 22 case against Rafa.

qs.q: Sol wants to reserve the civil action and file it separately. Can she?
o: Yes, before the prosecution presents evidence
No. In B.P. 22 cases, the civil action is deemed included and no reservation is allowed
Yes, if she pays the docket fees first
Only with the court's permission
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(b).

qs.q: How are filing fees handled for the civil aspect?
o: They are a first lien on the judgment
Sol pays fees based on the amount of the check when she files
No fees are required in criminal cases
Rafa pays them if convicted
qs.tw: Same B.P. 22 case.
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(b): the offended party pays filing fees based on the amount of the check involved.

qs.tw: Before the B.P. 22 case, Sol had already filed a civil collection case, and its trial has not started.
qs.q: What may happen to that civil case?
o: It must be dismissed
It may be consolidated with the criminal case upon application
It proceeds independently
It is automatically suspended forever
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(b): a separately filed civil action whose trial has not started may be consolidated with the criminal case on application.

qs.tw: Rafa files a counterclaim for damages against Sol in the B.P. 22 case.
o: Yes, since the civil action is included
No. Counterclaims, cross-claims, and third-party complaints are not allowed in the criminal case; file a separate civil action
Yes, if it arises from the same check
Only after conviction
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 1(a).

qs.tw: New case: Tomas is charged with estafa. Before the criminal case, a civil case was filed whose ruling would decide whether the criminal case can proceed. The criminal case is now in court.
qs.q: When must Tomas file his petition to suspend?
o: Any time before judgment
In the same criminal case, before the prosecution rests
Only during preliminary investigation
In the civil case
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 6.

qs.tw: Change it: Tomas filed that civil case only after the criminal case was filed.
o: Yes, if the issues are related
No. A prejudicial question needs a previously instituted civil action
Yes, if the civil case is decided first
Only if the court consolidates them
qs.ex: Rule 111, Sec. 7(a). The Continuous Trial Guidelines also treat a petition to suspend without a properly filed civil case as a prohibited motion.

S.title: Inside the preliminary investigation
S.base: Uma files a complaint for qualified theft (penalty far above 4 years, 2 months, and 1 day) with the city prosecutor against Vic.

qs.q: Vic receives a subpoena. Instead of a counter-affidavit, he files a motion to dismiss. Is that allowed?
o: Yes, any time
No. He must file a counter-affidavit within 10 days; a motion to dismiss in its place is not allowed
Yes, if he cites lack of jurisdiction
Only with leave
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 3(c).

qs.tw: Vic ignores the subpoena and files nothing.
qs.q: What does the investigating prosecutor do?
o: Wait until he appears
Resolve the complaint based on the complainant's evidence
Dismiss for lack of a counter-affidavit
Ask the court to compel him
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 3(d).

qs.tw: The investigating prosecutor finds probable cause and files the information without the city prosecutor's prior written approval.
o: None; any prosecutor may file
Lack of the head prosecutor's prior written authority — a ground to quash, which Vic must raise before plea
The information is void and cannot be cured
The court must dismiss it on its own
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 4; Rule 117, Sec. 3(d). Jurisprudence treats the defect as waivable.

qs.tw: The information is properly filed. Within 10 days, the RTC judge reads only the prosecutor's certification and issues a warrant.
o: Yes, the certification is enough
No. The judge must personally evaluate the prosecutor's resolution and its supporting evidence
Yes, the prosecutor already found probable cause
No, the judge must hold a full hearing with witnesses
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a). The judge need not personally examine witnesses, but cannot rely on the certification alone.

qs.tw: The judge has doubts about probable cause.
o: Dismiss right away
Order the prosecutor to present additional evidence within 5 days, and resolve within 30 days from filing
Conduct his own preliminary investigation
Refer the case to the DOJ
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a).

qs.tw: Instead, the evidence clearly fails to show probable cause.
o: Issue the warrant anyway
Immediately dismiss the case
Return the records to the prosecutor
Wait for a motion
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 5(a).

qs.tw: Rewind: the city prosecutor dismissed Uma's complaint. Uma petitions the Secretary of Justice, who reverses.
o: No, the city prosecutor's ruling is final
Yes. The Secretary of Justice may reverse or modify and direct the filing of an information
Only if the RTC approves
Only if Vic consents
qs.ex: Rule 112, Sec. 4.

S.title: Hot pursuit, methods, and escapes
S.base: Police arrive at a market ten minutes after a stabbing. They see the victim, hear eyewitnesses describe a man in a green shirt who just ran off, and find a man in a blood-stained green shirt nearby.

qs.q: Can they arrest him without a warrant?
o: No, they did not see the stabbing
Yes. The offense was just committed, and they have probable cause based on facts they personally gathered right away
Only if he confesses
Only with a barangay official present
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5(b): hot pursuit — offense just committed, plus probable cause based on personal knowledge of facts and circumstances.

qs.tw: Instead, police arrest him three days later, based only on a witness's statement.
o: Yes, under hot pursuit
No. The offense was not "just committed," and they lack personal knowledge; they need a warrant
Yes, because there is an eyewitness
Yes, within 7 days
qs.ex: Hot pursuit needs immediacy and personal knowledge.

qs.tw: Police get a warrant. The arresting officer does not have it with him. The suspect demands to see it.
o: No, the warrant must be in hand
Yes. The officer need not have it in his possession, but must show it as soon as practicable after the arrest if asked
Only if the suspect consents
No, the suspect may refuse
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 7.

qs.tw: The suspect runs into his house and refuses to open the door.
o: Wait for a search warrant
Break in, after announcing his authority and purpose and being refused admittance
Nothing; homes are inviolable
Only call the suspect's lawyer
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 11.

qs.tw: Different scene: a private citizen sees a man snatch a bag and grabs him.
o: No, only officers may arrest
Yes. A private person may arrest in the same situations, and must deliver him to the nearest police station or jail
Only with a barangay official
Only if the citizen is a lawyer
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 5.

qs.tw: The arrested man escapes from jail a week later.
qs.q: Do police need a warrant to recapture him?
o: Yes, a new warrant
No. An escaped person may be pursued and retaken without a warrant, at any time and anywhere in the Philippines
Only within the same city
Only within 24 hours
qs.ex: Rule 113, Sec. 13.

S.title: Bail: how it works day to day
S.base: Wena is charged with estafa (bailable as a matter of right). She is out on a property bond.

qs.q: Until when does her bail stay in force?
o: Until arraignment
At all stages until promulgation of the RTC judgment, unless cancelled
Until the prosecution rests
Until the case reaches the Supreme Court
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 2(a).

qs.tw: Wena, already arraigned, skips a trial date without justification despite notice.
o: It must be postponed until she appears
She is deemed to waive her right to be present; trial may proceed in absentia
The case is dismissed
She is automatically convicted
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 2(c); Rule 115, Sec. 1(c). Trial in absentia needs arraignment, notice, and unjustified absence.

qs.tw: The court declares her bond forfeited.
o: Pay immediately
Within 30 days, produce her and explain why judgment should not be rendered against them
Nothing; forfeiture is final
Ask for a new bond
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 21. If they fail, judgment is rendered against them jointly and severally.

qs.tw: Wena is acquitted.
o: The bondsmen must apply to cancel it
It is automatically cancelled
It stays until appeal
It is forfeited
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 22: automatically cancelled on acquittal, dismissal, or execution of a judgment of conviction.

qs.tw: Rewind: Wena could not post bail and has been detained for as long as the maximum imprisonment for the offense.
o: She stays until judgment
She is released immediately, without prejudice to the trial continuing
She must post a reduced bail
She is acquitted
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 16.

qs.tw: Out on bail, Wena tries to fly abroad without the court's permission.
qs.q: Can she be arrested without a warrant?
o: No, she has bail
Yes. An accused on bail may be re-arrested without a warrant if she tries to leave the Philippines without permission
Only by her bondsman
Only after her bail is cancelled
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 23.

qs.tw: Before arraignment, Wena (out on bail) moves to quash the warrant for lack of probable cause.
o: Yes, bail waives all objections
No. Bail does not bar challenges to the arrest, warrant, or PI if raised before plea
Yes, unless the bail was cash
Only if the prosecutor objects
qs.ex: Rule 114, Sec. 26.

qs.tw: New accused: Xyla, still at large and not arrested, files a petition for bail.
o: Yes, bail is a right
No. Bail requires that she be in the custody of the law
Yes, if she pays double
Only for light offenses
qs.ex: Jurisprudence (e.g., Paderanga v. CA): only a person in custody, by arrest or voluntary surrender, may apply for bail.

S.title: Pleas, plea bargaining, and pre-trial
S.base: Yuri is charged with murder. At arraignment, the victim's family (the offended party) and the prosecutor are present.

qs.q: Yuri offers to plead guilty to homicide. What is needed?
o: Only the judge's approval
Consent of the offended party and the prosecutor, and the court's approval
Only the prosecutor's consent
An amended information
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2: plea to a lesser offense necessarily included in the charge, with consent of the offended party and prosecutor. No amendment needed.

qs.tw: The offended party does not appear at arraignment despite due notice.
qs.q: Can the plea to homicide still be accepted?
o: No, the offended party must always consent
Yes, with the conformity of the trial prosecutor alone
Only after a postponement
Only if Yuri pays damages first
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 1(f).

qs.tw: Yuri pleaded not guilty at arraignment. Before trial, he wants to plead guilty to homicide.
o: Yes, after arraignment no change is allowed
No. After arraignment but before trial, he may withdraw his not-guilty plea and plead to the lesser offense
Only with a new information
Only during trial
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: Yuri pleaded guilty to homicide. Before the judgment becomes final, he says he did not understand the plea.
o: No, a guilty plea is final
Yes. The court may allow an improvident plea of guilty to be withdrawn any time before the judgment becomes final
Only before sentencing
Only on appeal
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 5.

qs.tw: Rewind: the information is vague about how Yuri took part. Before arraignment, he asks for a bill of particulars.
o: No, bills of particulars are for civil cases
Yes, if filed before arraignment and it specifies the defects and details wanted
Only after the prosecution rests
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 9.

qs.tw: At arraignment, Yuri appears unable to understand the charge because of an unsound mental condition.
o: Enter a not-guilty plea
Suspend the arraignment and order a mental examination
Proceed, because counsel is present
Dismiss the case
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 11(a).

qs.tw: Yuri stays outside the courtroom, and his lawyer enters a plea of not guilty for him.
o: Yes, counsel may plead for the accused
No. The accused must be present and personally enter his plea
Yes, if the court records it
Yes, for not-guilty pleas only
qs.ex: Rule 116, Sec. 1(b).

qs.tw: At pre-trial, Yuri's lawyer signs a written stipulation admitting Yuri was at the scene. Yuri does not sign it.
qs.q: Can the stipulation be used against Yuri?
o: Yes, counsel binds the client
No. Pre-trial admissions must be in writing and signed by both the accused and counsel
Yes, if the court approved it
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 118, Sec. 2.

S.title: More quash grounds and jeopardy exceptions
S.base: Zed is charged with a light offense. The information was filed after the offense had already prescribed.

o: The facts charged do not constitute an offense
The criminal action or liability has been extinguished
The court has no jurisdiction over his person
The information does not conform to the prescribed form
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(g). Prescription extinguishes criminal liability.

qs.tw: Zed raises prescription only on appeal, after conviction.
o: Yes, it should have been raised before plea
No. Extinction of liability is never waived
Yes, unless the prosecution agrees
Only on the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 9.

qs.tw: New case: an MTC tries Zed for an offense that belongs to the RTC. He is arraigned and convicted. The case is then refiled in the RTC.
qs.q: Is the RTC case barred by double jeopardy?
o: Yes, he was already convicted
No. The first court had no jurisdiction, so no jeopardy attached
Yes, because he was arraigned
No, but he gets credit for time served
qs.ex: First jeopardy needs a court of competent jurisdiction (Rule 117, Sec. 7). Lack of jurisdiction over the offense is never waived.

qs.tw: Zed was never validly arrested, but he posted bail, was arraigned, and only then moved to quash for lack of jurisdiction over his person.
o: Yes, jurisdiction over the person is never waived
No. He submitted to the court's jurisdiction and did not raise it before plea
Yes, because the arrest was invalid
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Lack of jurisdiction over the person is waivable (it is not among a, b, g, i). Objections must be raised before plea (Rule 114, Sec. 26; Rule 117, Sec. 9).

qs.tw: Zed was convicted of slight physical injuries after pleading guilty to that lesser offense without the prosecutor's or offended party's consent. He is now charged with serious physical injuries for the same act.
o: Yes, double jeopardy
No. A plea to a lesser offense without their consent does not bar the graver charge
Yes, unless new evidence appeared
No, but only if he consents
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(c). He is credited for any part of the sentence served.

qs.tw: Instead, the facts making up the graver offense existed at the time of his plea but were discovered only afterward.
o: Yes, the facts already existed
No. Facts discovered only after the plea allow the graver charge
Yes, unless he consents
Only if the victim died
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 7(b).

qs.tw: Different information: its own allegations show that Zed acted in lawful self-defense.
o: The facts do not constitute an offense
It contains averments that, if true, would be a legal excuse or justification
Lack of jurisdiction
Double jeopardy
qs.ex: Rule 117, Sec. 3(h).

S.title: Trial procedure and witnesses
S.base: Abel is on trial for homicide.

qs.q: Abel admits killing the victim but claims self-defense. Can the order of trial change?
o: No, the prosecution always goes first
Yes. When the accused admits the act but claims a lawful defense, the order may be modified (reverse trial)
Only if the prosecution agrees
Only in civil cases
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 11(e).

qs.tw: A key prosecution witness is about to leave the Philippines with no definite date of return.
qs.q: How can the testimony be preserved?
o: It cannot; wait for the witness
Conditional examination before the court where the case is pending, with Abel present or notified
By affidavit only
By deposition before a notary abroad
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 15.

qs.tw: Instead, a defense witness is sick and lives more than 100 km away with no means to travel.
qs.q: Before whom may the witness be conditionally examined?
o: Only the trial court
A judge, a member of the bar in good standing designated by the judge, or an inferior court judge
Any notary public
The prosecutor
qs.ex: Rule 119, Secs. 12–13.

qs.tw: A witness testified in an earlier case with the same parties and subject matter, where Abel cross-examined him. The witness has since died.
qs.q: Can that earlier testimony be used against Abel?
o: No, it violates confrontation
Yes. Prior testimony of an unavailable witness may be used where the adverse party had a chance to cross-examine
Only if Abel agrees
Only in the civil aspect
qs.ex: Rule 115, Sec. 1(f).

qs.tw: Before he was ever arraigned, a co-accused, Bart, escaped.
qs.q: Can Bart be tried in absentia?
o: Yes, trial in absentia is allowed for fugitives
No. Trial in absentia requires that the accused was first arraigned
Yes, if counsel is appointed
Yes, after 30 days
qs.ex: Constitution and Rule 115, Sec. 1(c): requisites are arraignment, due notice, and unjustified absence.

qs.tw: Trial has gone on for over 180 days because of prosecution delays. Abel never moved to dismiss before trial. Now, after trial, he moves to dismiss for violation of speedy trial.
qs.q: Will the motion prosper under Rule 119?
o: Yes, the 180-day limit was violated
No. Failure to move for dismissal before trial waives the right to dismissal under Rule 119, Sec. 9
Yes, automatically
Only with the prosecutor's consent
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 9. The constitutional right to speedy trial remains a separate basis (Sec. 10).

qs.tw: Different case: Cora is charged with estafa, but the evidence shows only theft, which is not included in estafa. Judgment has not yet been rendered.
o: Acquit her right away
Not discharge her if there is good cause to detain; commit her for the proper offense and dismiss the original case once the proper information is filed
Convict her of theft
Convict her of estafa
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 19.

qs.tw: Back to Abel. After both sides rest but before judgment, a new witness surfaces.
qs.q: Can the judge reopen the proceedings?
o: No, the case is submitted
Yes. Before finality of a judgment of conviction, the judge may reopen, motu proprio or on motion, with a hearing, to avoid miscarriage of justice
Only on the prosecution's motion
Only on appeal
qs.ex: Rule 119, Sec. 24. The reopened proceedings must end within 30 days.

S.title: Judgment contents, promulgation, and new trial
S.base: Bea is tried for theft in an RTC in Cebu.

qs.q: The judge acquits Bea, writing only: "The accused is not guilty." Is the judgment complete?
o: Yes, an acquittal needs no explanation
No. It must state whether the evidence absolutely failed or merely failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and whether the act giving rise to civil liability existed
Yes, if the prosecutor does not object
No, it must also fix the penalty
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: Rewind: Bea is convicted. She is detained in a Davao jail.
o: The Cebu judge must travel to Davao
The executive judge of the RTC with jurisdiction over the place of confinement, upon the Cebu court's request
Any Davao clerk of court
It must wait until she is brought to Cebu
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6.

qs.tw: Bea is in Cebu, but the judge is absent on the promulgation date.
o: Nobody; reset it
The clerk of court
The prosecutor
Bea's counsel
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6: the clerk may promulgate when the judge is absent or outside the province or city.

qs.tw: Different case: Bea is convicted of a light offense. She is absent, but her counsel is present.
o: No, she must be present
Yes. For a light offense, judgment may be pronounced in the presence of counsel or a representative
Only after a warrant is served
Only if she consents in writing
qs.ex: Rule 120, Sec. 6.

qs.tw: Back to the theft conviction. Bea moves for new trial, offering a witness she knew about before trial but did not call.
o: Yes, any new witness is enough
No. Evidence that could have been found and presented with reasonable diligence is not newly discovered
Yes, if the witness is credible
Only if the prosecutor agrees
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 2(b).

qs.tw: Instead, new trial is granted on truly newly discovered evidence.
qs.q: What happens to the evidence already presented?
o: It is all set aside
It stands; the new evidence is added
Only the defense evidence stands
Only documents stand
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 6(b).

qs.tw: Instead, new trial is granted because of an irregularity that prejudiced Bea at trial.
o: All evidence stands
The proceedings and evidence affected are set aside and taken anew
The case is dismissed
The judgment is affirmed
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 6(a).

qs.tw: The judgment has become final. Bea now moves for new trial in the RTC.
o: Yes, any time
No. New trial must be sought before the judgment of conviction becomes final
Yes, on newly discovered evidence
Only with the prosecutor's consent
qs.ex: Rule 121, Sec. 1.

S.title: Appeal routes and higher courts
S.base: Cris is convicted in a criminal case.

qs.q: Cris was convicted by an MTC, which followed the same procedure as an RTC. Where and how does he appeal?
o: To the CA by petition for review
To the RTC by notice of appeal
To the SC by certiorari
To the RTC by petition for review
qs.ex: Rule 122, Secs. 2(a), 3(a). Rule 123: MTCs follow the same procedure as RTCs, except RTC-only provisions and summary procedure.

qs.tw: The RTC affirms on appeal. Cris wants to go to the CA.
o: Notice of appeal
Petition for review under Rule 42
Petition for certiorari under Rule 65
Automatic review
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 3(b): from the RTC in its appellate jurisdiction.

qs.tw: Different case: Cris was tried by the RTC and sentenced to reclusion perpetua.
o: Petition for review on certiorari to the SC
Notice of appeal to the CA
Automatic review by the SC
Petition for review to the CA
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 3(c).

qs.tw: The CA affirms reclusion perpetua.
qs.q: How does he go to the SC?
o: Petition for review on certiorari
Notice of appeal filed with the CA
Automatic review
Motion for reconsideration only
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 13(c).

qs.tw: Instead, the CA affirms a 10-year sentence.
qs.q: How does he go to the SC?
o: Notice of appeal
Petition for review on certiorari (Rule 45)
Automatic review
Petition for review (Rule 42)
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 3(e); Rule 125, Sec. 2.

qs.tw: At the CA, Cris's counsel de oficio fails to file the appellant's brief on time.
qs.q: Can the CA dismiss the appeal for this?
o: Yes, failure to file a brief is always fatal
No. The CA may not dismiss for failure to file a brief when the appellant is represented by counsel de oficio
Yes, after 30 days
Only if the OSG asks
qs.ex: Rule 124, Sec. 8.

qs.tw: Back at the trial court, Cris filed a notice of appeal but now wants to withdraw it. The records have not yet been forwarded.
o: No, an appeal cannot be withdrawn
Yes. The trial court may allow it, and the judgment becomes final
Only with the CA's approval
Only if the prosecution agrees
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 12.

qs.tw: The offended party appeals only the amount of civil damages.
qs.q: Does this affect Cris's criminal conviction?
o: Yes, the whole case reopens
No. An appeal of the civil aspect does not affect the criminal aspect
Yes, the penalty may be increased
Only if Cris also appeals
qs.ex: Rule 122, Sec. 11(b).

qs.tw: While the appeal is pending at the CA, Cris discovers new evidence material to his defense.
